source.title: Notes on Nursing: What It Is, and What It Is Not
source.attribution: Florence Nightingale, Notes on Nursing: What It Is, and What It Is Not, Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Nightingale wrote her nursing notes for families, not just professionals
cards.body:
Florence Nightingale published Notes on Nursing in 1860, and she was clear about who it was for. Not a manual for trained nurses, she said, but hints for anyone who has charge of someone else's health, whether a child or an invalid. In her day that meant mostly women at home. Today it means almost all of us: the parent with a feverish toddler, the adult child looking after an ageing mother, the partner sitting up with someone after surgery.

She also refused to hand out rules. She wanted readers to think for themselves about the person in front of them. The ideas in these cards are offered in that spirit: ways of caring well alongside proper medical advice, never in place of it.
cards.quote: I do not pretend to teach her how, I ask her to teach herself, and for this purpose I venture to give her some hints.
cards.apply_it: Think of one person whose care you share or might one day share. What is one thing you could learn now that would help?

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say Notes on Nursing was meant to be?
options: Hints to help ordinary carers think for themselves
A training manual for hospital nurses
quiz.explanation: She wrote that the notes were not a manual but hints for anyone in charge of another person's health, so they could teach themselves.

cards.title: Caring for someone is far more than handing out their medicine
cards.body:
Nightingale noticed that people thought 'nursing' meant giving medicines and applying poultices. To her that was a small part of it. Real care, she wrote, is getting the basics right: fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet and the right food at the right time, all arranged so the sick person spends as little of their scarce energy as possible.

This still rings true at home. Medicines come from the doctor, but whether someone rests well also depends on a quiet room, a window they can see out of, a clean bed and meals they can face. These are the parts of care that fall to family, and they matter.
cards.quote: It ought to signify the proper use of fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet, and the proper selection and administration of diet--all at the least expense of vital power to the patient.
cards.locator: What It Is, and What It Is Not ¶10
cards.apply_it: Walk into the room of someone you care for and check the basics: air, light, warmth, quiet, cleanliness. Fix one thing.

quiz.question: Besides medicine, what did Nightingale say nursing should include?
options: Strict bed rest and nothing else
Fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet and good food
quiz.explanation: She listed fresh air, light, warmth, cleanliness, quiet and diet, all arranged to save the patient's strength.

cards.title: Let fresh air in, but keep the person you care for warm
cards.body:
Nightingale's first rule for a sickroom was fresh air. She was frustrated that people kept rooms sealed and stuffy for fear of the cold, and equally frustrated that others thought making a room freezing was the same as airing it. Her point was that the two are separate. You can open a window and still keep someone warm with blankets, warm clothing and a heated room.

Today that might mean airing a stuffy bedroom for a while each day while the person stays well covered, and making sure they are never left sitting in a draught. Fresh air and warmth together, not one at the expense of the other.
cards.quote: To have the air within as pure as the air without, it is not necessary, as often appears to be thought, to make it as cold.
cards.apply_it: Next time you air a sick person's room, add a blanket first and keep them out of the draught.

quiz.question: What mistake about fresh air did Nightingale point out?
options: Thinking fresh air must also mean a cold room
quiz.explanation: She wrote that keeping the air fresh does not require making the room cold; warmth and fresh air can go together.

cards.title: Ask what happens to the care when you are not there
cards.body:
Nightingale called it 'petty management': making sure that what you do when you are there still gets done when you are not. A devoted carer who never leaves the bedside, she argued, may give worse care than a less devoted one who plans well, because nobody can be there every hour.

So she suggested a simple question. I must be away on Tuesday, but quiet and regular meals matter just as much on Tuesday. At ten at night I am never in the room, but quiet matters just as much at ten. Whether you are caring for a parent, a child or a team, the gaps in your presence are where things slip.
cards.quote: At 10 P.M. I am never with my patient; but quiet is of no less consequence to him at 10 than it was at 5 minutes to 10.
cards.apply_it: List the hours this week when you won't be with the person you look after. For each one, who or what covers it?

quiz.question: What did Nightingale mean by 'petty management'?
options: Saving money on small household items
Telling servants off for small mistakes
Arranging that good care continues when you are absent
quiz.explanation: She defined it as knowing how to manage so that what you do when you are there is also done when you are not there.

cards.title: Tell them when you are going out and when you will be back
cards.body:
It can feel kinder to slip out quietly so a sick person doesn't fret about being left. Nightingale disagreed strongly. If you have to go, say so openly, and say when you will return, whether it's for a day or ten minutes.

If someone finds out you left without telling them, she warned, they stop trusting that things will be done while you're away. And if they don't know when you'll be back, they can't plan anything that depends on you. The same applies to children and to anyone who relies on you: a clear 'I'm going to the shop, back by four' is more reassuring than a quiet disappearance.
cards.quote: For the same reasons, always tell a patient and tell him beforehand when you are going out and when you will be back, whether it is for a day, an hour, or ten minutes.
cards.apply_it: The next time you leave someone who depends on you, tell them where you're going and when you'll be back, even for a short trip.

quiz.question: Why did Nightingale say you should not slip away without telling the patient?
options: They might want to come with you
If they find out, they stop trusting that things will be done while you're away
quiz.explanation: A patient who discovers you left without saying so will never feel secure that what depends on you will be done in your absence.

cards.title: Waiting and uncertainty can wear a sick person down more than effort
cards.body:
Nightingale noticed that what really drained sick people was not exertion but suspense: waiting for news, not knowing when someone would arrive, dreading a surprise. While you are thinking about other things, she wrote, they are lying there turning the same worry over and over.

Her rule was to settle things quickly. If a letter needs answering or a decision needs making, get it done so it's off their mind. Today that could mean giving someone the test result as soon as you have it, confirming a visit time rather than leaving it vague, or simply telling them what the plan for the day is.
cards.quote: Apprehension, uncertainty, waiting, expectation, fear of surprise, do a patient more harm than any exertion.
cards.apply_it: Is someone you know waiting on an answer from you? Give it to them today, even if it's only 'I'll know by Friday.'

quiz.question: According to Nightingale, what does a patient more harm than exertion?
quiz.explanation: She listed apprehension, uncertainty, waiting, expectation and fear of surprise as more harmful than any exertion.

cards.title: Being in charge means making sure everyone does their part
cards.body:
Nightingale thought few people understood what it means to be 'in charge'. It isn't doing everything yourself, she said, and it isn't handing out jobs and walking away. It is making sure the right things happen: that each person does the task they're given and nobody undoes it through carelessness.

She observed that one sick person waited on by four people could be worse looked after than many patients cared for by one, simply because nobody was really in charge. In a family sharing the care of a relative, or at work, the same holds: decide who is responsible, and then check that it happens.
cards.quote: It is neither to do everything yourself nor to appoint a number of people to each duty, but to ensure that each does that duty to which he is appointed.
cards.apply_it: If you share caring duties with others, write down who does what and agree on one person who checks it all happens.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say being 'in charge' really means?
options: Giving orders and leaving others to it
Ensuring each person carries out the duty they are given
quiz.explanation: She said it is neither doing everything yourself nor just appointing people, but ensuring each does their appointed duty.

cards.title: Take pride in a system that runs smoothly without you
cards.body:
Some people, Nightingale noticed, liked the feeling that they would be missed: nobody else understood their system, their accounts or their way of doing things. She thought the real pride lay in the opposite. Keep things so clear that anyone could pick them up, so that if you fall ill or have to go away, everything carries on as usual.

For a family carer this might mean a written list of medications and times, the doctor's number on the fridge, and notes on what the person likes to eat. For a manager it's good handover notes. Being irreplaceable is not the goal; being covered is.
cards.quote: so that, in case of absence or illness, one can deliver every thing up to others and know that all will go on as usual, and that one shall never be missed.
cards.apply_it: Write a one-page handover for something only you know how to do, so someone else could step in tomorrow.

quiz.question: Where did Nightingale think the real pride of someone in charge should lie?
options: In being the only one who understands the system
In keeping things so clear that others could carry them on
quiz.explanation: She believed the pride should be in a system anyone could understand and carry on, so that one would never be missed.

cards.title: Whispering near someone who is ill is harder on them than ordinary talk
cards.body:
Nightingale observed that sick people often coped with loud, steady noise, like building work outside, far better than with a whisper. What hurts, she wrote, is noise that creates expectation: a familiar voice murmuring outside the door, or a hushed conversation in the room that they can't quite catch.

A whisper makes the listener strain to hear, especially when they suspect they're the subject. So if you need to talk, speak normally within their hearing or go well out of earshot. Don't hover halfway, half-hiding a conversation they can tell is about them.
cards.quote: If it is a whispered conversation in the same room, then it is absolutely cruel; for it is impossible that the patient's attention should not be involuntarily strained to hear.
cards.apply_it: Next time you need to discuss someone's care, either include them openly or move right out of earshot.

quiz.question: Why did Nightingale consider whispering in a sick room so harmful?
options: The patient can't help straining to hear it
It is impolite to the doctor
quiz.explanation: She wrote that the patient's attention is involuntarily strained to hear a whispered conversation, which wears them out.

cards.title: Don't discuss someone's condition just outside their door
cards.body:
Nightingale singled out one habit as perhaps the worst of all: a doctor or friend leaving the bedside and then giving their opinion on the visit to the family just outside the door, or in the next room, where the patient can hear or knows it is happening.

The person in bed is left lying there, guessing what is being said about their own body. Today the same thing happens in hospital corridors and on phone calls in the hallway. If news needs sharing, find a truly private place, or better, include the person who is ill when that's what they would want.
cards.quote: for a doctor or friend to leave the patient and communicate his opinion on the result of his visit to the friends just outside the patient's door
cards.apply_it: If you're about to discuss a loved one's health, check: can they hear this, or know it's happening? If so, move or include them.

quiz.question: Which habit did Nightingale call 'if possible, worst of all'?
options: Discussing the patient's condition just outside their door
quiz.explanation: Giving opinions just outside the door, within the patient's hearing or knowledge, was in her view the worst kind of unnecessary noise.

cards.title: Protect a sick person's first sleep of the night
cards.body:
Nightingale treated an unbroken first sleep as close to sacred. Wake someone who is ill soon after they drop off, she warned, and they may lose not just that sleep but the ability to get back to sleep at all. Woken after a few hours, they are much more likely to drift off again.

She also noticed that, unlike healthy people, the sick often sleep better the more they sleep. In practice: plan noisy jobs, phone calls and visitors around their rest, check the door doesn't bang, and don't wake them just to ask how they are. If a doctor has said to wake them for medicine, follow that.
cards.quote: If he is roused out of his first sleep, he is almost certain to have no more sleep.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, before the person you care for settles, sort anything noisy that might disturb them in their first hour of sleep.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say happens when a sick person is woken from their first sleep?
options: They sleep longer the next night
They are almost certain to get no more sleep
quiz.explanation: She wrote that a patient roused from their first sleep is almost certain to have no more sleep that night.

cards.title: Slowness is not the same as gentleness
cards.body:
It seems considerate to tiptoe around a sick person and move very slowly. Nightingale thought it did the opposite. Lingering, shuffling steps and a hesitant touch keep the person waiting and watching. What they need is a firm, light, quick step and a steady, quick hand.

You can be brisk and gentle at the same time. Come in, do what's needed calmly and competently, and let them rest. The same is true when comforting a child or helping someone after an operation: a confident, unhurried but efficient manner is more soothing than nervous creeping about.
cards.quote: Slowness is not gentleness, though it is often mistaken for such: quickness, lightness, and gentleness are quite compatible.
cards.apply_it: Notice how you move around someone who is unwell. Try a light, steady pace rather than tiptoeing or rushing.

quiz.question: What manner did Nightingale recommend around the sick?
options: A firm, light, quick step and a steady hand
Staying completely still in a corner
quiz.explanation: She said slowness is often mistaken for gentleness, but quickness, lightness and gentleness go together.

cards.title: Sit down where they can see you and give them your full attention
cards.body:
Nightingale had precise advice for visitors. When a sick person talks to you about something that matters to them, sit down. Don't stand fidgeting, don't show signs of hurry, give your full attention, and leave as soon as the subject is finished.

She added: sit where they can see you without turning their head, and don't make them keep looking up at you standing over them. Everybody looks at the person who is speaking, and for someone weak that small effort adds up. Taking a chair at their eye level tells them you are really there.
cards.quote: Always sit down when a sick person is talking business to you, show no signs of hurry give complete attention and full consideration if your advice is wanted, and go away the moment the subject is ended.
cards.apply_it: On your next visit to someone unwell, pull up a chair within their line of sight before you start talking.

quiz.question: Where did Nightingale say a visitor should sit?
options: On the end of the bed
Within the patient's view so they need not turn their head
By the door, ready to leave
quiz.explanation: She advised sitting within the patient's view so they don't have to turn their head or keep raising their eyes to see you.

cards.title: Don't stop someone to talk while they're on their feet
cards.body:
When a weak person is making their way from bed to chair or along a corridor, Nightingale warned, don't meet them halfway to deliver a message. She had seen a patient fall flat because someone came in and spoke while he was standing. You have no idea, she wrote, what effort it is for a weak person to stay standing even a few seconds to listen.

Wait until they've sat down. Ten seconds or ten yards, and their walk is over. This applies to anyone frail or recovering, including older relatives: let them reach their seat before you ask a question.
cards.quote: You do not know the effort it is to a patient to remain standing for even a quarter of a minute to listen to you.
cards.apply_it: When someone frail is moving about, hold your question until they're seated.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale advise when a weak patient is walking across the room?
options: Wait until they have sat down before speaking to them
Walk beside them and chat to keep their spirits up
Hand them their letters on the way
Ask them to stop and rest standing up
quiz.explanation: Standing even briefly to listen is a real effort for a weak patient, so she said to wait until their walk is over.

cards.title: Judge how a visit went by how they are afterwards
cards.body:
A lively hour of conversation can make someone who is ill seem much brighter than they are. Nightingale's advice: never judge a sick person's real state from how they look during an animated visit. Come back and see them an hour after, and find out how they slept that night.

She noticed that the effects of over-exertion nearly always show up later, not during the effort. So a visitor who says 'It did them good, they were so chatty!' may be mistaken. For anyone with a long illness or easily drained energy, plan shorter visits and check how they fare the next day.
cards.quote: Indeed, almost every effect of over-exertion appears after, not during such exertion.
cards.apply_it: After someone you care for has had visitors, check in with them later or the next day and ask how tired they felt.

quiz.question: When did Nightingale say the effects of over-exertion usually appear?
options: Never in people who are resting in bed
quiz.explanation: She wrote that almost every effect of over-exertion appears after, not during, the exertion, so judge a visit by its aftermath.

cards.title: Keep your doubts to yourself and bring them a clear decision
cards.body:
Nightingale believed people who are ill need conciseness and decision above almost anything. Whatever uncertainty you feel, sort it out in your own head. What they should hear is the conclusion, not every twist of your thinking.

She noticed that changing your mind wore patients out more than facing even a hard decision. Suggest a trip to one place in the morning and another in the afternoon, and they have imagined themselves in both. If you care for someone, think things through, check with others if needed, and then present one clear plan.
cards.quote: Let your doubt be to yourself, your decision to them.
cards.apply_it: Before your next conversation about plans with someone unwell, settle your own thinking first and bring them one clear option.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say patients dread most in the people around them?
quiz.explanation: She wrote that irresolution is what patients most dread, and that a change of mind injures them more than a hard decision.

cards.title: If you read aloud to someone who is ill, read slowly or just tell it
cards.body:
People often rush through reading to a sick person to get it over with. Nightingale thought that was a great mistake. Read slowly, clearly and steadily, fairly loud but not noisy, and above all not for too long. Patients often say 'Don't read it to me, tell it me,' and she noted that sick children nearly always prefer a story told to one read.

She also disliked the habit of reading silently to yourself and then reading out odd bits now and then. The listener is left waiting in the gaps. Choose what to share and give it your full attention.
cards.quote: Reading aloud to the sick ought always to be rather slow, and exceedingly distinct, but not mouthing--rather monotonous, but not sing song--rather loud but not noisy--and, above all, not too long.
cards.apply_it: Next time you read to a child or someone unwell, slow down, keep it short, or try telling the story in your own words.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say about reading aloud to the sick?
options: Read as fast as possible to save their energy
Read slowly and distinctly, and not for too long
quiz.explanation: She advised reading rather slowly, very distinctly, not too loud, and above all not too long.

cards.title: Bring slow variety to someone stuck with the same four walls
cards.body:
Nightingale thought few healthy people could imagine how much the sick suffer from staring at the same walls and ceiling day after day. She believed the most depressed patients were often those surrounded by the same unchanging objects.

But variety must be slow. Show someone a dozen pictures at once and you tire them out. Hang one new picture opposite the bed each day or each week, and they will enjoy the change. Today that might be a new photo on the wall, a card on the windowsill, moving the bed or chair to a different view, or a fresh plant now and then.
cards.quote: hang one up opposite him, one on each successive day, or week, or month, and he will revel in the variety.
cards.apply_it: Change one thing in the view of someone who is housebound this week: a picture, a photo, a plant or where their chair faces.

quiz.question: How did Nightingale say variety should be given to the sick?
options: All at once, to make a big impression
Only when they ask for it
By moving them to a new room every day
Slowly, one new thing at a time
quiz.explanation: She warned that many pictures at once could exhaust a patient, but one new one each day or week would be enjoyed.

cards.title: Flowers and bright colour can lift someone who is ill
cards.body:
Nightingale was a fever patient herself, and she never forgot it. She wrote about the agony of patients unable to see out of a window, with only knots in the wooden walls to look at, and the delight of fever patients over a bunch of bright flowers. When someone sent her a posy of wild flowers, she felt her recovery speed up from that moment.

She insisted that beauty, colour and variety were not just a fancy of the sick but a real help to them. A bunch of flowers, a colourful blanket or a bright picture is a simple gift. Check first if a hospital ward allows flowers.
cards.quote: I remember (in my own case) a nosegay of wild flowers being sent me, and from that moment recovery becoming more rapid.
cards.apply_it: Send or bring something bright to someone who is unwell: flowers, a picture, or a colourful card.

quiz.question: What happened, in Nightingale's own experience, when she was sent wild flowers while ill?
options: She felt her recovery became more rapid
She asked for them to be removed
She gave them to another patient
quiz.explanation: She recalled that from the moment a posy of wild flowers was sent to her, her recovery became more rapid.

cards.title: Someone who is ill is using more self-control than you can see
cards.body:
Healthy people sometimes think the sick could simply 'dismiss painful thoughts' with a little more willpower. Nightingale pushed back hard. Almost any sick person who behaves decently, she wrote, is exercising more self-control every moment than you will know until you are ill yourself. Every step across the room may hurt them, and so may every thought.

She offered a comparison: imagine being up all night and then told to exercise self-control instead of getting your cup of tea. That is how a sick person's nerves feel all the time. Before judging someone as irritable or low, remember what it costs them just to be polite.
cards.quote: if he can speak without being savage, and look without being unpleasant, he is exercising self-control.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone unwell who has been short with you. What effort might they be making that you can't see?

quiz.question: What did Nightingale compare the state of a sick person's nerves to?
options: How yours feel after you have been up all night
quiz.explanation: She wrote that the nerves of the sick are always in the state yours are in after being up all night.

cards.title: Watch for the hours when they can actually eat
cards.body:
Nightingale knew that many weak patients simply couldn't face food at the usual mealtimes. A heavy breakfast might be impossible, while the same meal at another hour would go down gladly. A patient who couldn't touch dinner at two might accept it at seven.

She told of a man saved from sinking by one simple question from his doctor: 'But is there no hour when you feel you could eat?' He could, at certain times. Patients rarely volunteer this, she noted, so it's up to the carer to watch and find out. Keep an eye on when appetite comes, and be flexible with the clock.
cards.quote: Patients very seldom, however, can tell this; it is for you to watch and find it out.
cards.apply_it: Ask the person you care for, or watch over a few days: is there a time of day when eating feels easier?

quiz.question: What simple question did Nightingale say helped save a patient who wasn't eating?
options: Have you tried eating more vegetables?
Is there no hour when you feel you could eat?
Why won't you eat your dinner?
quiz.explanation: The doctor's question about whether there was any hour the patient could eat led to meals at those times, and it worked.

cards.title: Bring food at the right time and take it away, eaten or not
cards.body:
It seems helpful to leave a plate by the bed in case the person feels like a bite later. Nightingale saw it put patients off food entirely. Bring the meal at the right time, she said, and take it away at the right time, eaten or uneaten. A plate that sits there all day only kills what appetite there is.

She also warned against fussing around the room, dusting or chatting about food, while someone is trying to eat. Let them eat in peace. (This is about plates of food; follow medical advice on keeping a drink within reach.)
cards.quote: Let the food come at the right time, and be taken away, eaten or uneaten, at the right time; but never let a patient have 'something always standing' by him, if you don't wish to disgust him of everything.
cards.apply_it: Next meal you bring someone, set a time to collect the plate, and leave them to eat without bustle.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say about leaving untouched food by a patient's bed?
options: It can put them off food altogether
It should always be done at night
quiz.explanation: She warned that leaving food standing by the patient tends to disgust them of everything; bring it and take it away at the right times.

cards.title: Put their bed where they can see the sky
cards.body:
After fresh air, Nightingale wrote, what sick people need most is light, and not just light but sunshine. She thought healthy people forgot that a sickroom is not like a bedroom. A healthy sleeper is only in bed at night, so the view doesn't matter. Someone ill may lie there all day.

So she urged that a sick person be able to see out of a window from bed without raising or turning themselves, to see sky and sunlight at least. She noticed that patients nearly always lie facing the light. Moving a bed or chair nearer a window is one of the simplest kindnesses there is.
cards.quote: that they should be able, without raising themselves or turning in bed, to see out of window from their beds, to see sky and sun-light at least, if you can show them nothing else
cards.apply_it: Check whether the person you care for can see out of a window from where they rest. If not, can you move the bed or chair?

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say was a sick person's greatest need after fresh air?
quiz.explanation: She wrote that second only to their need of fresh air is their need of light, and direct sunlight in particular.

cards.title: Don't put off helping someone get clean, and wash your own hands often
cards.body:
Nightingale noted that one of the most common sights at any sickbed is the relief a person feels once their skin has been carefully washed and dried. She warned carers not to postpone it on the grounds that it's 'only' comfort and can wait. Fresh skin and clean clothes after sweating are part of good care, not an extra.

She had a short instruction for the carer too: wash your hands very often through the day. Both still hold. Help the person you look after stay clean and dry, keep it warm and private so they don't get chilled, and keep your own hands clean.
cards.quote: Every nurse ought to be careful to wash her hands very frequently during the day.
cards.apply_it: Today, wash your hands before and after each time you help someone who is ill.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say carers should not do about a patient's washing?
options: Put it off because it only brings a little relief
quiz.explanation: She warned against delaying washing on the plea that all it gives is a little relief; the comfort is real and matters.

cards.title: Don't accept 'what can't be cured must be endured' as an excuse
cards.body:
Nightingale had no patience with resignation from the person giving care. The saying 'What can't be cured must be endured' was, she wrote, the worst and most dangerous maxim a nurse could live by. Patience is a virtue in your own troubles, but patience with a fixable problem in someone else's care is just carelessness under another name.

A draught, a noisy neighbour, an uncomfortable chair: to the sick person who can't move, these are real burdens. If you're looking after someone, keep asking whether the thing everyone has got used to could actually be changed.
cards.quote: 'What can't be cured must be endured,' is the very worst and most dangerous maxim for a nurse which ever was made.
cards.locator: X. Cleanliness of Rooms and Walls ¶32
cards.apply_it: Name one small problem in someone's care that everyone has accepted. What would it take to fix it this week?

quiz.question: How did Nightingale view the maxim 'What can't be cured must be endured' for a carer?
options: As the worst and most dangerous maxim for a nurse
As wise advice for hard times
As a good motto for patients
quiz.explanation: She called it the very worst and most dangerous maxim for a nurse, since resignation in a carer amounts to carelessness.

cards.title: Spare people who are ill your cheerful false hopes
cards.body:
Nightingale had a chapter called 'Chattering Hopes and Advices', and she spoke from long experience, including her own illness. There is hardly a greater burden for the sick, she wrote, than the relentless hopes of their friends: making light of the danger and exaggerating the chances of recovery.

These visitors mean well, but the person in bed is not cheered. Either they wear themselves out explaining why they are worse, or they say nothing and feel alone. For someone with a long or serious illness, honest company is a gift. Listen to how they see it rather than telling them how it will turn out.
cards.quote: I really believe there is scarcely a greater worry which invalids have to endure than the incurable hopes of their friends.
cards.apply_it: Next time you visit someone seriously ill, swap 'You'll be fine' for a question: 'How are you finding things?'

quiz.question: What did Nightingale call one of the greatest worries the sick endure?
options: The incurable hopes of their friends
quiz.explanation: She wrote there is scarcely a greater worry for invalids than the incurable hopes of their friends who try to 'cheer' them.

cards.title: They have probably heard your advice fifty times already
cards.body:
Everyone, Nightingale complained, feels entitled to advise a sick person: try this place, this doctor, this tonic, this exercise. Often the advice comes from people who know far less than the doctor who has been treating them for months, and they never ask about the patient's real condition first.

Her gentle point: the person has very likely heard the same suggestion fifty times, and if it were practical they'd have tried it long ago. Before offering a cure or tip to someone with a long illness, ask yourself if they asked for it. Usually what helps more is to ask how they are and listen.
cards.quote: it is probable the patient has heard such advice at least fifty times before, and that, had it been practicable, it would have been practised long ago.
cards.apply_it: The next time you feel the urge to suggest a remedy to someone who's ill, ask a question instead.

quiz.question: Why did Nightingale think unsolicited advice to the sick was usually useless?
options: Advice should only come in writing
They have likely heard it many times and would have tried it if it were practical
quiz.explanation: She pointed out that the patient has probably heard the advice fifty times, and if it were workable it would have been tried.

cards.title: Remember to bring them good news, not only your worries
cards.body:
Nightingale noticed visitors who left the sick person to carry the whole conversation, then said they'd forgotten to mention the pleasant news. She didn't object to sharing your anxieties; she thought that could be good for both of you. But if you can remember your worries, she said, you can remember good news too.

She found the sick loved hearing of real things going well: a romance heading somewhere happy, a kind act that actually worked. Such news was, she wrote, 'like a day's health'. Today, before visiting or calling, jot down a few good things from your week to share.
cards.quote: if you tell him what is anxious, surely you can remember to tell him what is pleasant too.
cards.apply_it: Before your next call or visit to someone unwell, write down two pieces of good news to tell them.

quiz.question: What kind of news did Nightingale say sick people especially enjoy?
options: Real, practical successes and things going well
quiz.explanation: She said a sick person loves to hear of real practical success, such as a kind act that worked, 'like a day's health' to them.

cards.title: A baby or a pet can brighten a sickroom
cards.body:
Nightingale wrote that there is no better company for each other than babies and sick people, as long as you arrange it so neither suffers. Seeing 'the baby' freshened a sick person's whole outlook, and a young child would usually adapt to the invalid's ways if the visit wasn't too long. She also thought a small pet could be a wonderful companion in a long illness, especially if the person could care for it themselves.

For families today, a short visit from a grandchild can mean a lot. Keep visits brief, and keep a young child away if the illness could spread to them.
cards.quote: It freshens up a sick person's whole mental atmosphere to see 'the baby.'
cards.apply_it: If a relative is ill at home and it's safe, arrange a short visit from a little one or a pet.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say about babies and sick people?
options: They should always be kept apart
Babies tire the sick too much
They are excellent company for one another if managed well
quiz.explanation: She wrote there is no better society than babies and sick people for one another, managed so neither suffers.

cards.title: Learn to observe: it is the most important practical skill in caring
cards.body:
If Nightingale had one lesson above all, it was observation. The most important practical thing anyone caring for the sick can learn, she wrote, is what to notice, how to notice it, which signs show improvement and which the opposite, which matter and which don't.

She was scornful of the question 'Is he better?' answered with a vague opinion. What helps is facts. For a family carer, that means paying attention to how much someone ate, how they slept, what they can and can't do compared with last week. Noticing well is what lets you speak up when something changes.
cards.quote: The most important practical lesson that can be given to nurses is to teach them what to observe--how to observe--what symptoms indicate improvement--what the reverse--which are of importance--which are of none--which are the evidence of neglect--and of what kind of neglect.
cards.apply_it: For the next three days, jot one line each evening about how the person you care for ate, slept and moved.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale call the most important practical lesson for nurses?
options: How to cook for the sick
quiz.explanation: She wrote that the most important practical lesson is teaching nurses what to observe and how to observe it.

cards.title: Ask precise questions, not leading ones
cards.body:
'Did you have a good night?' sounds caring, but Nightingale thought it was nearly useless. One person calls a night bad if they didn't sleep ten straight hours; another calls it fine after a few short dozes. She knew of two patients given the same answer, one of whom had barely slept for five days.

Better to ask: How many hours did you sleep, and when? Precise questions get truer answers, she wrote, partly because people shy away from correcting a leading question. The same works with appetite, pain or a child's day at school: ask for specifics.
cards.quote: Lies, intentional and unintentional, are much seldomer told in answer to precise than to leading questions.
cards.apply_it: Replace one 'Did you have a good night?' today with 'Roughly how many hours did you sleep?'

quiz.question: Why did Nightingale dislike questions like 'Has he had a good night?'
options: They are leading and produce vague, misleading answers
They take too long to answer
quiz.explanation: She showed that leading questions gather inaccurate information, while precise ones such as how many hours of sleep get truer answers.

cards.title: 'You look so well' can be the wrong thing to say
cards.body:
Nightingale warned that the face is one of the least reliable guides to how someone really is. She had known patients in terrible pain and exhaustion keep a healthy colour almost to the end, and heard them greeted over and over with 'I am glad to see you looking so well', followed by suggestions to take more exercise.

People with long or invisible illnesses still hear this today, and it can leave them feeling unseen. Instead of commenting on how someone looks, ask how they are feeling, and believe what they tell you.
cards.quote: And scores of times have I heard these unfortunate creatures assailed with, 'I am glad to see you looking so well.'
cards.apply_it: Next time you greet someone who is unwell, skip comments on their looks and ask, 'How are you feeling today?'

quiz.question: Why did Nightingale distrust the remark 'You look so well'?
options: Patients prefer to be told they look ill
It is only acceptable from doctors
The face often tells the least about how someone really is
quiz.explanation: She wrote that the face is perhaps the part of the body that tells the casual visitor least, and seriously ill people may still look healthy.

cards.title: Notice what they can no longer do so they don't have to tell you
cards.body:
Nightingale thought few things weighed so heavily on someone with a long, incurable illness as having to keep explaining, in words, that they can no longer do something they could do a month or a year ago. A carer's job, she wrote, is to notice this without being told.

She also saw the danger of not noticing. A patient who could get out of the bath alone last month may not manage now, and a carer who assumes otherwise can leave them stranded. Keep quietly watching what has changed, and adjust help before they have to ask.
cards.quote: What is a nurse there for if she cannot observe these things for herself?
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you care for: what could they do a few months ago that they find harder now? Is your help keeping up?

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say presses heavily on someone with a long illness?
options: Having to keep telling the nurse what they can no longer do
quiz.explanation: She wrote that having to record in words for the nurse each new thing they can no longer do is a heavy burden on the patient.

cards.title: Check on them soon after they first get up from a spell in bed
cards.body:
When someone has been in bed for a few days and gets up for the first time, Nightingale warned, they are almost certain to feel faint, cold or need something. Yet carers would let them walk into another room and not look in on them.

The excuse was often 'He doesn't like to be fussed over.' Perhaps he said so weeks ago when he was well, she replied, but that was not this situation. If needed, find a reason to pop in. For an older relative home from hospital, or anyone first up after illness, stay close at first and check on them a few minutes later.
cards.quote: It never occurs to her that he is quite certain to be faint, or cold, or to want something.
cards.apply_it: When someone you look after first gets up after illness, stay nearby and check on them within a few minutes.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say about a patient getting up for the first time after some days in bed?
options: They should be left alone to build confidence
They should walk as far as possible
They will usually feel much better
They are likely to be faint, cold or need something, so check on them
quiz.explanation: She warned that such a patient is quite certain to be faint, cold or in want of something, and should be looked in on.

cards.title: Some people want company when ill; others want to be left alone
cards.body:
Nightingale urged carers to notice what kind of person they were caring for. One wants to suffer quietly and be looked after as little as possible. Another wants to be made a fuss of, pitied, and have someone always nearby. Both preferences, she thought, deserve to be noticed and honoured far more than they are.

Too often the first person gets constant fussing they hate, while the second is left feeling neglected. Don't care for someone the way you would want to be cared for. Watch, or ask, how they want it.
cards.quote: One likes to suffer out all his suffering alone, to be as little looked after as possible. Another likes to be perpetually made much of and pitied, and to have some one always by him.
cards.apply_it: Ask the person you care for directly: would you like more company right now, or more time to yourself?

quiz.question: What mistake did Nightingale say carers often make about patients' preferences?
options: Fussing over those who want to be left alone and neglecting those who want company
Letting them choose their own visitors
quiz.explanation: She noted that busy attention is often forced on the patient who wants to be let alone, while the one who wants company feels neglected.

cards.title: Give the doctor your facts, not just your opinion
cards.body:
Nightingale saw that the doctor often visits once a day, usually at the same time, and may see someone at their best. The person who is with them through the night knows things the doctor cannot. But telling a doctor 'He was dying all night!' doesn't help much. What the doctor needs is the facts.

That is still the most useful thing a family carer can bring to an appointment: what happened, when, how much they ate, how many hours they slept, what has changed. She noted that a doctor who cares will soon value someone who observes carefully and reports clearly.
cards.quote: What he wants is not your opinion, however respectfully given, but your facts.
cards.apply_it: Before the next medical appointment, write three short factual notes about what you've observed, with times and amounts.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say a doctor most needs from the carer?
options: A list of remedies they have tried
Reassurance that the patient is fine
quiz.explanation: She wrote that the doctor wants not your opinion, however respectfully given, but your facts.

cards.title: Children feel everything that affects a sick adult, only more
cards.body:
Nightingale ended her book by returning to children. Everything she had written about caring for the sick applied to them even more, she said. Children are affected by the same things as adults, but more quickly and more seriously: stuffy rooms, cold, startling noises, being woken roughly, irregular meals, dullness and lack of light, too many or too few covers, and carers who don't plan.

For parents of a poorly child, that means the basics count double. Keep the room calm, warm and airy, avoid sudden noises and jolts, keep meals and rest regular, and watch them closely. Always follow medical advice for anything worrying.
cards.quote: They are affected by the same things, but much more quickly and seriously
cards.apply_it: When your child is next unwell, check their room against her list: air, warmth, quiet, light, regular rest and meals.

quiz.question: How did Nightingale say children respond compared with adults to the conditions around them?
options: Less, because they are more resilient
Only to noise, not to anything else
quiz.explanation: She wrote that children are affected by the same things as adults, but much more quickly and seriously.

cards.title: With a baby, everything depends on how carefully you watch
cards.body:
An adult can tell you where it hurts. A baby can't. Nightingale pointed out that with infants, everything depends on the accurate observation of the mother or nurse who has to report to the doctor, and she lamented how rarely that accuracy was achieved.

She valued training the eye. She liked the idea of a game where a father and son walked past a toy shop window, then each listed everything they had seen and went back to check. For a parent today it can be as simple as noting feeds, nappies, sleep and temperature when a baby is unwell, so you can give the doctor a clear picture.
cards.quote: In the case of infants, _everything_ must depend upon the accurate observation of the nurse or mother who has to report.
cards.apply_it: If your baby or young child is unwell, keep a simple log of feeds, sleep and anything unusual to share with the doctor.

quiz.question: Why did Nightingale say observation matters especially with infants?
options: Everything depends on the observation of the person who reports for them
quiz.explanation: Because infants can't describe their symptoms, she wrote that everything depends on the accurate observation of the mother or nurse.

cards.title: A good carer doesn't play doctor with medicines
cards.body:
Nightingale did not want carers giving out medicines on their own judgment. She was alarmed by people handing round old prescriptions to friends and neighbours, or giving children strong medicines without a doctor. Her ideal carer was the opposite: the experienced, observant nurse who 'neither physics herself nor others'. If medicine is to be given, she said, send for the doctor.

That principle is as sound as ever. Your role is to watch closely, keep the person comfortable and report clearly. Don't share prescription medicines or change doses yourself; check with a doctor or pharmacist.
cards.quote: she neither physics herself nor others.
cards.apply_it: Check your home medicine cupboard: are any prescription medicines there that belong to someone else or are out of date? Ask a pharmacist how to dispose of them.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale say the experienced, observant nurse does about medicines?
options: Gives them freely to anyone who is ill
Neither doses herself nor others without the doctor
quiz.explanation: She wrote that the experienced and observing nurse 'neither physics herself nor others', and advised sending for the doctor.

cards.title: Do the good thing, whatever people say you should or shouldn't do
cards.body:
Notes on Nursing ends with a plea to women of her day. Nightingale asked them to ignore two kinds of talk: one that urged women to do everything men did simply because men did it, and one that told them to stay away from certain work simply because they were women. Both, she said, were just listening to 'what people will say'.

Her advice was to bring the best you have to the work in front of you. A good deed isn't better because it's surprising a woman did it, nor worse because someone thinks it unsuitable. The principle travels well: judge your work by whether it does good, not by others' expectations.
cards.quote: But you want to do the thing that is good, whether it is 'suitable for a woman' or not.
cards.apply_it: Is there something good you've held back from because of what people might think? Take one small step toward it this week.

quiz.question: What did Nightingale urge her readers to do about the opinions of others on 'women's work'?
options: Follow whichever view was most popular
Ignore both sides and do the good that was in front of them
quiz.explanation: She asked women to leave both 'jargons' aside and do the good thing, whether it was thought 'suitable for a woman' or not.
